title: Blip 04: Dialogue Voices, a Village Cast
shortText: 104 dialogue blips: 13 village speakers for cozy, farming and RPG games, none an earlier Blip voice. Same cues.
html:
A village cast of dialogue voices

104 dialogue sounds. 13 new speakers, each a different synthesis method.

The ticks and chirps a text box plays as a line types out, for the people of a village in a cozy, farming or RPG game: a baker, a blacksmith, a carpenter, a farmer, a fisher, a florist, an innkeeper, a librarian, a mayor, a miller, a peddler, a doctor and the mail carrier. It works on its own, and it is built to sit beside Blip 01, Blip 02 and Blip 03 without ever sounding like them: same 8 cues, same file names, 13 new voices.

Licence, up front

Royalty free. Commercial use. No credit required. No revenue limit, no unit cap, no second licence to buy later if your game does well. Use it in as many projects as you like, on any platform. The one thing you may not do is resell the sounds themselves as sounds. The full plain language terms ship as LICENSE.txt, with a copy paste credit line if you want one.

Everything is synthesised from code. No recordings, no sample libraries, no third party clips, so there is no upstream licence behind this one and nobody can content ID claim these sounds against your project.

Hear it first

There is a free demo on this page with four complete voices, chosen by measurement from the darkest to the brightest end of the cast, all 8 cues each, copied unaltered. Play them back to back before you pay.

The new cast

  • Peddler. Bold and persuasive. A brassy tone that opens up as it speaks. 384 Hz
  • Carpenter. Steady and practical. A hollow wooden knock at the pitch of the voice. 390 Hz
  • Baker. Warm and round. A soft tone with a gentle shimmer inside it. 401 Hz
  • Librarian. Quiet and careful. A soft murmur made of tiny grains of tone. 481 Hz
  • Blacksmith. Strong and direct. Every glyph rings like a light hammer on an anvil. 595 Hz
  • Mayor. Grand and a little pompous. Three voices at once, slightly apart, like speaking to a crowd. 743 Hz
  • Doctor. Brisk and precise. The pitch flutters inside every glyph. 878 Hz
  • Farmer. Plain and friendly. A low, natural buzz. 1009 Hz
  • Innkeeper. Gruff and welcoming. A low hum with a hollow notch carved out of it. 1018 Hz
  • Miller. Old and slow. A deep creak that rattles through every glyph. 1246 Hz
  • Florist. Light and quick. A thin, bright whistle of a voice. 1697 Hz
  • Fisher. Easy going, a voice from the dock. Every glyph is a little wet gloop. 2791 Hz
  • Mail Carrier. Cheerful and on the move. A narrow, reedy buzz. 3613 Hz

A narrow noise band, a trill, a narrow pulse, amplitude modulation, a bubble, a wood block, an anvil, brass FM, a glottal pulse, grains, a notch, a chorus and vocal fry. The figures are the mean brightness of each voice's own per glyph tick, measured off the shipped WAV files. What each description says is measured too: 20 of 20 claims hold when measured again from the files, the anvil's ring, the innkeeper's notch, the mayor's three voices, the miller's rattle and the rest.

Four packs, 52 voices, no collisions

Inside this pack all 78 pairs of voices are separated by at least 12 percent in brightness or 25 percent in length. Across the series the same check runs over all four casts together: 52 voices, 1326 pairs, 507 of them a new voice against an earlier Blip voice, and 1326 of 1326 are separated. The check is proven to fire: each earlier voice planted back in as a re pitched copy was caught, 39 of

  1. The result ships as series_proof.json.

Every speaker ships the same 8 cues as Blip 01, 02 and 03

  • blip_01. tick for one glyph, take 1
  • blip_02. tick for one glyph, take 2
  • blip_03. tick for one glyph, take 3
  • soft. the same voice pitched lower, for asides and whispers
  • loud. the same voice pitched higher and held longer, for shouting and emphasis
  • question. rising inflection, for a line ending in ?
  • exclaim. emphatic hit, for a line ending in !
  • advance. page turn / next line, in this voice

File names are voice then cue, exactly as in the earlier packs, so a dialogue system already wired for any earlier Blip pack takes these voices by changing the speaker id and nothing else.

Fit

  • WAV and OGG for every file, 16 bit, 44.1 kHz, mono.
  • One loudness band. The inner 80 percent sits inside 0.87 dB, so switching speaker never changes how loud the text box is. The soft and loud cues differ in pitch and length, not level, so set their volume in your game for a real whisper or shout.
  • Slow speakers by design. Peddler, Mayor, Innkeeper and Miller tick for 150 ms or more; fire them every third glyph, or once per word.
  • 13 declared variation sets, three takes per voice, so a repeated tick never repeats a file.
  • Nothing loops, and no file carries loop points.
  • pack_proof.json ships with the pack: 945 checks, 0 failed.

Honest limits

These are synthesised character voices in the blip tradition, not recorded speech and not a vocal synthesiser. They say that someone is talking; they do not say words. The measurements above are signal measurements, not a claim that it sounds good. That is what the free demo is for.

AI disclosure, stated truthfully: the code that generates these sounds was written with AI assistance. The sounds themselves are self contained procedural synthesis, oscillators, filters and delay lines evaluated in code, with no generative audio model at any point. The cover art and store graphics are AI generated.

More voices from the same studio

  • Blip 01: Dialogue Voices for Text Advance, the first cast, fantasy speakers.
  • Blip 02: Dialogue Voices, a Second Cast, sci fi and fantasy speakers.
  • Blip 03: Dialogue Voices, a Third Cast, modern and school speakers.
  • Babble 01: Dialogue Voices, speakers that talk in made up syllables instead of ticks.
